patient.chief_complaint: 2-year progressive triad: shuffling gait, urinary incontinence, and forgetfulness
patient.history_present_illness: A 73-year-old retired engineer with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation of a classic 2-year progressive triad: (1) Shuffling magnetic gait that has progressively worsened — he requires a cane and has had four falls in 6 months, including a hip bruise. His wife describes him as 'walking like his feet are glued to the floor.' (2) Progressive urinary urgency and incontinence — he wears pads daily and has nocturnal incontinence. (3) Progressive forgetfulness — his wife reports he frequently repeats himself, forgets recent conversations, and has become slow in decision-making. MMSE outpatient was 24/30. MRI obtained by his primary care physician shows 'significant ventriculomegaly' with reported Evans index 0.38. He was referred to neurology inpatient for tap trial. He has no features of Alzheimer's disease (no prominent episodic amnesia isolated to encoding), no tremor or rigidity (argues against Parkinson's), and no orthostatic hypotension. All three triad symptoms began progressively over 2 years in a compatible timeframe.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. MoCA 22/30 — loses primarily on trail-making, recall, and clock drawing. Frontal-subcortical pattern. No aphasia.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength throughout. No tremor. No rigidity.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles (age-appropriate). Joint position intact.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Classic magnetic gait — short shuffling steps, wide base, markedly reduced foot clearance, en bloc turning requiring 8-10 steps. Gait freezing at doorways. TUG 28 seconds. 10-meter walk 22 seconds. Cannot tandem walk.
neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel rigidity. No postural tremor. Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers. No orthostatic hypotension on standing.

signal_characteristics.description: Classic tight high-convexity sulci with disproportionate sylvian fissure widening
Callosal angle 72 degrees on coronal imaging
Thinning and upward bowing of corpus callosum
Prominent aqueductal flow void on sagittal T1
Periventricular T2/FLAIR signal ('halo' of transependymal CSF seepage)

mri.impression: Classic textbook NPH imaging: Evans index 0.38, callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH pattern, corpus callosum thinning and upward bowing, aqueductal flow void, periventricular transependymal signal. Highly supportive of idiopathic NPH. Clinical correlation recommended.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 12 cmH2O. WBC: 1 cell/mcL (N/A PMN/N/A lymph). Protein: 38 mg/dL. Glucose: 66 mg/dL (ratio 0.70). cytology: No malignant cells. beta_amyloid_42: 862 pg/mL (normal). total_tau: 178 pg/mL (normal). phospho_tau: 26 pg/mL (normal).

specialized_test.test_type: High-volume tap trial (45 mL) with gait analysis and cognitive testing

findings.gait_description: Post-tap at 24h: markedly improved step height, longer steps, less freezing, better turns in 5-6 steps (vs 8-10 pre-tap)

specialized_test.impression: Strongly positive tap trial: 36% TUG improvement, 32% 10m walk improvement, and 3-point MoCA improvement at 24 hours. This is a clearly positive tap trial that strongly predicts VP shunt response. Diagnosis of idiopathic NPH confirmed. Urgent neurosurgery referral for VP shunt with pressure-adjustable valve.
recommended_actions: Urgent neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt
Pressure-adjustable valve to optimize post-shunt drainage

output.impression: Markedly hyperdynamic aqueductal CSF flow (peak velocity 28 cm/s — well above 18 cm/s threshold). This objective finding strongly supports NPH pathophysiology and the robust tap trial response. VP shunt is strongly indicated.

findings.result: Negative amyloid PET — CL score 6 (well below threshold of 24.4)

output.impression: Clearly negative amyloid PET. No Alzheimer's copathology. Combined with normal CSF biomarkers, Alzheimer's disease is excluded. Shunt prognosis is excellent.
recommended_actions: VP shunt with excellent prognosis given negative amyloid PET

output.test_type: Neuropsychological evaluation pre and post tap
output.impression: Significant neuropsychological improvement post-tap, particularly in frontal-subcortical domains (executive function, processing speed). Memory also improved. Pattern is consistent with NPH diagnosis with excellent prognosis for shunting. Cognitive improvement of this magnitude (3 MoCA points, 6 ADAS-cog points) strongly predicts sustained benefit from VP shunt.
recommended_actions: VP shunt with favorable cognitive prognosis

findings.finding: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity (NDO) — involuntary contractions at 170 mL fill
No outlet obstruction despite age (no BPH pattern)

output.impression: Classic neurogenic detrusor overactivity from NPH-related frontal inhibitory pathway dysfunction. No outlet obstruction. This pattern is expected to improve after VP shunting.
recommended_actions: VP shunt expected to improve NDO

output.test_type: Extended 72h lumbar drainage (offered as option for further prognostication; not required given strongly positive tap trial)
output.impression: Extended drainage demonstrates progressive and sustained improvement to 45% TUG reduction — the best possible predictor of VP shunt response. This patient will likely have excellent and durable neurological improvement with shunting.

output.proposed: Perioperative management for VP shunt: cefazolin prophylaxis
interactions: Amlodipine: continue perioperatively; discuss with anesthesia for BP management
Rosuvastatin: continue perioperatively — no surgical interaction
warnings: Amlodipine may cause perioperative hypotension — have vasopressors available

differential.key_features: Cognitive decline — but negative amyloid PET, normal CSF biomarkers, and frontal-subcortical cognitive pattern argue strongly against AD
Gait disorder — but no tremor, no rigidity, ventriculomegaly
Hypertension — but minimal white matter disease, Evans 0.38 with DESH

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI — Evans index, callosal angle, DESH pattern
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Classic NPH: Evans 0.38, callosal angle 72, DESH, transependymal signal

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive labs to exclude reversible causes
High-volume tap trial (45 mL) with gait assessment and cognitive testing
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal pressure 12 cmH2O; strongly positive tap — 36% TUG, 3 MoCA points

critical_actions: Formal gait analysis (TUG and 10m walk) BEFORE and AFTER tap trial — mandatory
Classic NPH triad + Evans 0.38 + callosal angle 72 + DESH = high-confidence diagnosis
Strongly positive tap trial (36% TUG, 3 MoCA points) confirms diagnosis and predicts excellent shunt response
Negative amyloid PET provides additional favorable prognostic information
contraindicated_actions: Diagnosing as Alzheimer's disease given cognitive decline without imaging and tap trial
Diagnosing as Parkinson's disease without tremor or rigidity
Attributing gait to 'old age' without formal workup
key_reasoning_points: Classic textbook NPH: 73-year-old man with 2-year progressive Hakim's triad (gait, incontinence, cognition)
Evans index 0.38 (well above 0.3 threshold), callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH — classic NPH imaging
Normal opening pressure (12 cmH2O) and normal CSF are required for NPH diagnosis
Strongly positive tap trial (36% TUG improvement, 3 MoCA points) — best predictor of shunt response
Negative amyloid PET and normal CSF biomarkers exclude Alzheimer's copathology — excellent prognosis
VP shunt with pressure-adjustable valve is the definitive treatment

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Classic textbook straightforward NPH: 73-year-old man with complete Hakim's triad, Evans 0.38, callosal angle 72, DESH pattern, strongly positive tap trial (36%), negative amyloid PET.
